---
title: "The laws"
---

{{< include ../_setup.qmd >}}

Every refusal you have met in this book is a consequence, not a policy. Nine
laws sit under the whole grammar, and each one exists to refuse a specific
temptation: something another tool does, that costs its users more than it
gives them. This chapter collects the laws in one place, with the temptation
beside each, because the vocabulary above them will grow and these will not.

## One word, one meaning

`by` groups, wherever it appears. `as` names, wherever it appears. `where`
asks, wherever it appears. The temptation is the convenience argument, a
word that means roughly similar things in different places; the cost is that
a reader can never again be sure, and checks the manual for the rest of
their life. You met this law working in the chapter on the small words, and
it is the reason a verb you have never seen is mostly made of words you
have.

## One way to say it

No `ascending` beside the default, no `drop` beside `keep`, no `distinct`
beside `pick` and `drop_duplicates`, no second spelling of anything.
Synonyms read as generosity and cost every reader a doubt: if both exist,
they must differ, so what is the difference? Where you catch this grammar
saying one thing two ways, that is a bug, and the afterword says where to
report it.

## Say the subject

A condition about a column's name writes `name`; about its kind writes
`kind`; the column under work in a sweep writes `value`. And where the
grammar has to decide something you did not say, it prints the decision
back. The sentence below is written in the text form, so the call is the
same string in both tabs:

::: {.panel-tabset}

### R

```{r}
#| message: true
run('marks then widen name [question], value [mark]')
```

### Python

```{python}
run('marks then widen name [question], value [mark]')
```

:::

The line above the table is the law at work: the grouping was assumed, and
the assumption was said aloud rather than exercised in private. Nothing in
this grammar decides quietly.

## A step is one step

No value in a step can read a column made beside it, and no name can be
made twice in one step. The temptation is the one-liner; the cost is a
hidden pipeline inside the line, where written order silently becomes
execution order. [Adding a column](adding-a-column.qmd) stages the first
refusal and names the second, which only the text form can spell.

## Nothing runs until you ask

A pipeline is a plan. Building one costs nothing, printing it runs it, and
`collect` hands over the table. The temptation this refuses is eager
execution, where every intermediate step materializes whether or not anyone
wanted it; the chapter that opens this part shows what the plan buys.

## Every refusal is the grammar's

One checker reads the whole pipeline before anything runs, so every message
in every language is written by the same voice, names the step you wrote,
and carries its repair. The temptation is delegating errors to whatever
engine hits the problem first, which is how a beginner meets a Java stack
trace with their column name somewhere inside it. The previous chapter is
this law's whole demonstration.

## The answer is settled

`drop_duplicates` returns a settled order. Windows that walk rows demand a
`sort` first. A grouped `take` without an order is refused. The temptation
is "whatever order the engine liked today", which is invisible until the day
two runs of one pipeline disagree and a test you trusted goes quiet. If an
answer could vary, the grammar either settles it or asks you to.

## It writes what you could have written

`show_as` renders any pipeline as dplyr, pandas, polars, PySpark, two
dialects of SQL, or the grammar itself, and the printed code is executed by
this project's own checks, not merely printed. The temptation being refused
is on the other side of the fence this time: a tool that holds your work
hostage to its own continued existence. The whole argument for adopting a
small grammar stands on this exit being real, and it has [its own
chapter](what-it-wrote.qmd).

## Your table stays yours

god has no table type, no session state, and no import format. A pandas
frame goes in and a pandas frame comes out; an R data frame likewise; a
Spark frame stays on its cluster. The temptation is the platform move,
where the price of the grammar is migrating your data into it. There is
nothing to migrate into, which is also why walking away from god costs one
`show_as` per pipeline.

## What the laws are for

None of these laws is about data. They are about what a person can retain,
which is the promise this book opened with: a grammar with no exceptions is
the only kind that survives a year of not being used. The laws are how the
promise is enforced against the vocabulary's own growth, and they bind the
author before they bind you. A proposed word that would break one does not
get in, however useful its best day looks.
